Rain improves Dhaka’s air quality
item.description:
Dhaka's air quality was marked "moderate" Saturday morning due to rain in the capital city.
With an air quality index (AQI) score of 124 at 9:17am, Dhaka ranked 13th on the list of world cities with the worst air quality.
Pakistan’s Lahore, India’s Delhi and Afghanistan’s Kabul occupied the first three spots in the list, with AQI scores of 267, 133 and 195, respectively.
An AQI between 0 and 50 is considered to be "good" while between 50 and 100 it is considered "moderate", while an AQI between 101 and 200 is considered "unhealthy", particularly for sensitive groups.
Similarly, an AQI between 201 and 300 is said to be "poor'", while a reading of 301 to 400 is considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks to residents.
AQI, an index for reporting daily air quality, is used by government agencies to inform people how safe or polluted the air of a certain city is, and what associated health effects might be a concern for them.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is based on five criteria pollutants -- Particulate Matter (PM10 and PM2.5), NO2, CO, SO2 and Ozone.
Dhaka has long been grappling with air pollution issues. Its air quality usually turns unhealthy in winter and improves during the monsoon.
Air pollution consistently ranks among the top risk factors for death and disability worldwide.
As per the World Health Organization (WHO), air pollution kills an estimated seven million people worldwide every year, largely as a result of increased mortality from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

The Rooppur reactor is ours. The fuel cycle isn't
item.description:
On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at 3:16 PM, a controlled chain reaction on the bank of the Padma pushed 350 megawatts into the national grid.
Fifty years of waiting ended in a control room full of engineers who had probably stopped believing they would live to see it. Whatever else is true about Rooppur, that moment belongs to them, and to the country that paid for it.
What is happening to the bill for that moment is another matter.
The Tk26,181 crore increase in the project's cost is real, and it is almost entirely a currency story. The Russian credit was denominated in dollars at a projected Tk80; the rate is now Tk 122.40, and the taka lost more than 30% of its value after 2022.
Anyone presenting that arithmetic as a corruption story either cannot do the sum or is counting on you not doing it. The post-August 5 regime has been counting. 16 months into a mandate built on accountability, it has an Anti-Corruption Commission file alleging Tk590 billion in embezzlement, a figure repeated until it sounds like a finding, and no charge sheet a court has tested.
Rosatom denies the allegations and says procurement followed both countries' laws. Let that argument run its course. What cannot wait is the thing nobody is shouting about.
A reactor that runs is not a country that chooses. In October, five months after the first fuel assemblies went into the core, Dhaka signed a five-page memorandum with Washington on nuclear cooperation. It is non-binding. It creates no obligations. A document that obligates nobody is not a framework, it is a photograph of an intention.
Read it next to February's trade agreement and the picture sharpens. Bangladesh got its tariff cut, from 20% to 19%, worth roughly $85m a year on current export volumes. In exchange, the text commits Dhaka not to buy reactors, fuel rods, or enriched uranium from any country that jeopardizes essential US interests, with a narrow exception where an existing reactor has no alternative supplier. Article 4.3 lets Washington terminate the whole arrangement if Bangladesh enters a preferential trading relationship with a non-market economy.
Rooppur runs a Russian VVER-1200. Western reactors use different geometries and enrichment specifications, and conversion is economically prohibitive.
Every 12-18 months the core needs fresh fuel, and that fuel comes from Russia. The first reload falls due in 2027 or 2028. No clause in any of these documents hands Washington a veto tomorrow. What it hands Washington is a date, a supplier constraint, and a legal instrument, all timed to the moment our reactor becomes dependent and our leverage disappears. We did not sell a veto. We leased one.
The global order is fracturing, and middle powers are learning to work the fracture. The Hedgers , published by Cambridge in March, describes the method: Take what each power offers, concede in communiqués, never concede in contracts.
India is the model. It buys discounted Russian crude, keeps Russian spares flowing, deepens semiconductor and defense-technology ties with Washington, and gives ground in language it can withdraw later.
Bangladesh did the opposite, and did it in all three directions at once. Russian fuel, Chinese payment plumbing, American permission. We called it balancing. It was stacking: Three dependencies laid on top of each other until the whole structure rested on nothing that was ours.
Even the payment workaround is failing. CIPS was supposed to let us settle with Moscow in yuan. It has not. Banks in Dhaka and in China have both flinched at the sanctions exposure, instalments sit in a Sonali Bank account that cannot be moved, and Moscow now talks about rupees and a Russian bank branch in the capital. The plumbing exists on paper and jams in practice, which is what happens when you build a bypass out of other people's infrastructure.
Washington has done this before, and closer to home. In 1971 it sailed the USS Enterprise into the Bay of Bengal for no reason a Bangladeshi needs explained. Financial architecture is simply the quieter version of the same gesture.
None of this is a case for abandoning Rooppur, and it is certainly not a case for defaulting on the IMF. It is a case for spending the next 18 months differently.
Start with Moscow, where we have more leverage than we use. The delays hurt Rosatom too, and Russia has already waived penalties on the project and pushed the first principal repayment back to September 2028, which is not the behaviour of a creditor with no stake in keeping the reactor alive.
Dhaka should be asking now, formally and publicly, for a longer grace period and a restructuring of the repayment curve, and should ask as a partner with a working reactor rather than as a supplicant with a problem.
Then capture what the plant actually earns. Fully operational, Rooppur displaces billions of dollars of imported LNG and furnace oil every year. That is foreign exchange that currently vanishes into the fuel bill and will now stay home.
It should not be absorbed into general revenue and spent. It should be ring-fenced into a debt-servicing fund with statutory protection, so that the plant pays for itself and builds the buffer we will need the first time the taka slips again.
And diversify the balance sheet before the reload window closes. Bangladesh has been a shareholder in the New Development Bank since 2021 and has drawn on it; the bank is targeting $30bn of approvals across 2022 to 2026, with a rising share in local currencies.
Partner status in the BRICS architecture should be a standing diplomatic ask rather than an occasional communiqué line, and local-currency settlement with India and China should move from aspiration to agreement. India's caution about expansion is a real constraint. It is not a reason to stop asking.
This reactor will light homes for 60 years. We waited half a century for it, borrowed to build it, and are now being asked to trade the keys to its fuel cycle for a tariff cut that rounds to nothing.
The current is flowing. The country is not yet in the control room.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst, and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal.

item.title: Justice for the Rohingya
item.description:
We are pleased to see that nearly a decade after Myanmar's brutal military crackdown in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has delivered a landmark judgment, finding Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya community.
For the Rohingya, this has been a long and painful wait, and while it is undoubtedly a historic decision, it's also one that must lead to more than international condemnation.
The atrocities are not unknown: Thousands of Rohingya civilians were killed or subjected to widespread sexual violence and extreme brutality, and entire villages were destroyed.
These were not isolated incidents of violence. They were part of a systematic campaign against a vulnerable ethnic minority whose very existence was repeatedly denied.
For Bangladesh, this judgment carries particular significance. We have borne an enormous humanitarian and economic responsibility by sheltering more than a million Rohingya refugees for years despite stretched resources, yet the prospect of safe repatriation continues to look distant.
Bangladesh cannot be expected to shoulder this responsibility indefinitely while Myanmar evades accountability.
The ruling must now be followed by meaningful international action. The ICJ has called on Myanmar to facilitate the safe return of refugees and make reparations to victims. However, a court judgment alone cannot guarantee either.
The international community must now do its part to put pressure on Myanmar's military leadership, demand cooperation with investigations, and ensure that those responsible face consequences. Regional powers must also stop treating the crisis as a diplomatic inconvenience.
Repatriation must also be handled with care. Rohingya refugees cannot be sent back into the same conditions that forced them to flee. Their safety, citizenship rights, freedom of movement, and dignity must be guaranteed.
For too long, the Rohingya have been denied justice, identity and a place to call home. This judgment is an important step towards accountability; now the world must ensure it is not also the end of the effort.

item.title: UNICEF launches ‘Chain of Hope’ campaign for 60m children
item.description:
UNICEF on Thursday launched the Chain of Hope, a national campaign to turn political commitments into concrete action for Bangladesh's 60 million children, during a visit by Sanjay Wijesekera, the organization's regional director for Asia and the Pacific.
Launched on the eve of World Children's Day, the campaign is anchored in the Government of Bangladesh's Five-Year Strategic Framework for Reform and Development (July 2026–June 2031). It aims to translate national commitments into measurable results for children.
Building on the Child Rights Manifesto, endorsed by 12 political parties in December 2025, the campaign will mobilize parliamentarians, partners, communities, young people and the private sector around 5 priorities: advancing adolescent girls' rights, ending child labor, ensuring birth registration for every child, protecting children from climate change and tackling lead poisoning.
The campaign will advocate for policy reforms and stronger services, including closing legal loopholes that permit child marriage, integrating birth registration into public services to reach the 4 in 10 children under 5 whose births remain unregistered, making schools and health facilities more climate-resilient, and developing a strategy to end child labor.
Progress will be tracked against campaign milestones, with a report scheduled for publication by the end of December 2027.
The campaign's name draws on the image of Bangladesh's 60 million children holding hands to symbolically form a chain of hope around the world, united by their rights and aspirations.
“Every girl and every boy in Bangladesh deserves to grow up healthy, safe and protected, with the opportunity to learn and reach their full potential,” Wijesekera said.
“Yet too many children are still denied these rights. Through the Chain of Hope, we want to turn commitments into real changes in children's lives, backed by policies, resources and accountability. Because every child deserves more than promises. Every child deserves action.”
The urgency is reflected in the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS 2025), which found that 47.2% of women aged 20–24 were married before the age of 18, while 9.2% of children aged 5–17 were involved in child labor.
The survey also found that only 59.2% of children under 5 had their births registered and that 38.4% of children aged 12–59 months had elevated blood lead levels.
During his 5-day visit to Bangladesh, Wijesekera met with Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, Speaker of the National Parliament; Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Finance and Planning; and Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury, Foreign Secretary.
The meetings focused on national priorities for children and opportunities to translate commitments into action.
In Dhaka's Korail area, Wijesekera visited a UNICEF-supported Child Protection Community Hub, an Aalo Clinic and a wastewater treatment facility. He also met young peer leaders working to protect children in their communities.
He engaged with young climate activists, child journalists and members of UNICEF's Young People's Advisory Group, highlighting the importance of children's voices in decisions affecting their future.
In Cox's Bazar, Wijesekera visited learning, health and nutrition services in Rohingya refugee camps, witnessing how declining humanitarian funding threatens essential services for more than half a million children.
“Throughout my visit, from the communities of Dhaka to Cox's Bazar, I witnessed both the immense challenges children face and their extraordinary determination to build a better future,” Wijesekera said.
“Bangladesh's commitment to improving children's lives presents a critical opportunity for meaningful change.”

item.title: Rain disrupts life in Satkhira, farmers fear crop losses
item.description:
Unseasonal rain has disrupted normal life in Satkhira, leaving daily wage earners and farmers struggling while raising concerns over potential damage to standing Aman paddy and mustard crops.
Rain began on Thursday morning and continued until Friday, bringing daily activities to a halt in several areas. Persistent showers and overcast skies affected the livelihoods of day-labourers and van and rickshaw pullers, many of whom struggled to find work or passengers.
The rain has also raised concerns among farmers over the harvesting of mature Aman paddy and the cultivation of mustard. However, the agriculture department said it was too early to assess the extent of possible damage.
Golam Rasul, a farmer from Kalaroa, said he had been preparing to harvest his paddy when the rain began. “If water accumulates in the fields, mature paddy and mustard seedlings could be damaged. We cannot work in the fields until the rain stops,” he said.
Gopal Das, a van puller from Rajarbagan in Satkhira town, said the rain had reduced the number of passengers. “There is hardly any work. After spending the whole day in the rain looking for passengers, it is difficult to earn enough to meet household expenses,” he said.
Plabani Sarkar, agriculture officer of Satkhira Sadar upazila, said the rain had started only that morning, making an immediate damage assessment impossible. She said rainfall could continue until Sunday and that the extent of damage could only be determined at least two days after the weather improved.
Late-planted Aman paddy is yet to be harvested and could face delays. Strong winds could cause mature plants to bend, affecting grain quality and yield. Mustard seedlings planted 15-20 days ago could also suffer damage if water remains stagnant for 36 hours or longer. Farmers have been advised to dig drainage channels to remove excess water from their fields.
Zulfikar Ali Ripon, acting officer of the Satkhira Meteorological Office, said 40mm of rainfall was recorded on Thursday. Light to moderate rain continued on Friday. Temperatures could fall to around 18-19 degrees Celsius, although a significant drop is not expected.
Meanwhile, experts have warned that sudden temperature fluctuations and damp weather could increase the risk of seasonal illnesses. High humidity, reportedly exceeding 90%, may create favourable conditions for viral, bacterial and fungal infections.

Two injured in crude bomb explosion in Kushtia
item.description:
Two men were severely injured after a crude bomb was hurled near them while they were unloading a bag of scrap material at a shop in the Mozampur area of Kushtia town on Friday afternoon.
The explosion occurred around 2:15pm near the railway line.
The injured were identified as scrap seller Suman from the Kotpara area and shop owner Ruhul Amin from Jagati Palpara.
Suman brought a bag of scrap materials on a rickshaw from Custom More to Ruhul’s shop. The blast occurred immediately as the bag was unloaded, triggering panic in the area, police and witnesses said.
Locals rescued the victims and rushed them to Kushtia General Hospital. Resident Medical Officer (RMO), Dr Iqbal Hasan of the hospital, said both sustained deep leg injuries and are receiving treatment in the surgery ward.
Officer-in-Charge Zakir Hossain of Kushtia Model Police Station, said police inspected the scene and collected evidence. He added that the victims will be questioned after recovery to determine the cause of the explosion.

item.title: PM: Armed Forces symbol of independence, sovereignty and pride
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has described the Armed Forces as a symbol of Bangladesh’s independence, sovereignty, pride and valour, saying they remain a vital national institution built on courage and discipline.
In a message issued on Friday ahead of Armed Forces Day on November 21, he said the history of the Army, Navy and Air Force was closely linked to the country’s birth and their role in the 1971 Liberation War.
Recalling November 21, 1971, the prime minister said members of the three services, alongside the Mukti Bahini, paramilitary forces and patriotic citizens, launched a coordinated counter-offensive against the Pakistani occupation forces. The day is observed annually as Armed Forces Day.
Tarique extended greetings to members of the Army, Navy and Air Force, and paid tribute to those who sacrificed their lives for the country, particularly the seven Bir Shreshthas.
He said the Armed Forces continue to protect the country’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity while enhancing Bangladesh’s international standing through their contributions to UN peacekeeping missions.
He also praised their role in responding to natural disasters and emergencies, saying they had earned public confidence through their service.
The prime minister recalled the contributions of former president Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Khaleda Zia to the development and modernisation of the Armed Forces.
He said the present government was taking comprehensive steps to develop a modern, technology-driven and efficient force in line with international standards.
Tarique also highlighted the Armed Forces’ role during the 2024 mass uprising and wished success to all programmes marking Armed Forces Day.

item.title: Rashed alleges Hasina’s forged signature in letter seeking passport, NID
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Political Assistant Rashed Khan has alleged that a forged signature of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina was used in an authorisation letter submitted to the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi in connection with her efforts to get a new passport and national identity card.
London-based law firm Matrix Chambers approached the High Commission with a power of attorney bearing Hasina’s purported signature, seeking to represent her in the matter.
The signature came under scrutiny as Sheikh Hasina is generally known to sign official documents in Bengali rather than English.
In a Facebook post on Thursday night, Rashed alleged that the signature on the authorisation letter had been forged.
“I have spoken in detail with an official working at the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi about this matter. After verification, they found evidence of signature forgery in the letter,” he wrote.
Rashed said Hasina had used a Bengali signature on all documents during her tenure as Prime Minister.
“Hasina is one person, and she should have only one signature. Even in applications of this kind, a signature other than the one previously used or recognised in the NID cannot be used. Nor is there any scope for using a forged signature,” he said.
Meanwhile, Barrister Steven Powles of Matrix Chambers sent another letter to the acting High Commissioner of Bangladesh in New Delhi on Thursday, seeking an update on his earlier letter seeking a passport and NID card for Hasina.
A certification from Hasina was also attached to the latest letter, according to the information available.
Rashed further alleged that Matrix Chambers had made a mistake while attempting to forge Hasina’s signature.
“Thieves always leave some trace behind. Matrix Chambers, the London-based law firm, made the same mistake while sending the letter with a forged signature of Sheikh Hasina. They could at least have asked her once whether she signs in Bengali or English,” he wrote.
Rashed also questioned whether Hasina did not understand English well or whether the lawyers at Matrix Chambers were unfamiliar with Bengali.

item.title: BGB foils BSF attempt to push in 4 through Meherpur border
item.description:
The Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) foiled an attempt by the Border Security Force (BSF) of India to push four unidentified men into Bangladesh through the border in Gangni upazila of Meherpur district early Friday.
According to a BGB, the incident took place around 2am in the area under the jurisdiction of Rangmahal Border Outpost (BOP) of Kushtia Battalion (47 BGB).
The attempt was detected and thwarted due to intelligence information, the alert presence of BGB patrol teams along the border and their prompt action.
Later, following the firm stance and effective initiatives of the Kushtia Battalion commander, BSF's Dighalkandi camp under its 11th Battalion took the four men back inside India's barbed-wire fence around 7:45am.
Kushtia Battalion Commander Lt Col Rashed Kamal Rony said regular patrols had been strengthened in the border area.
He said BGB personnel were maintaining the highest level of vigilance and professionalism to ensure overall border security.

item.title: Mintoo urges people to cooperate with law enforcement agencies
item.description:
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo on Friday urged people not to take the law into their own hands but to cooperate with the law enforcement agencies.
"We have been victims of oppression and persecution for the past 17 years. The people have supported us and brought us to power. The nation is currently at peace, and we wish to maintain that peace," he said while speaking as the chief guest at a meeting held at Daganbhuiyan Upazila Parishad auditorium in Feni.
Mintoo said those, who are legally banned, are trying to create anarchy in the country but they will not be allowed to do so in any way.
The minister said those involved in past acts of oppression and current illegal activities must be brought to justice, cautioning that no innocent person should be harassed out of personal vendetta.
Calling upon all abide by laws, Mintoo asked BNP leaders and activists to inform law enforcement immediately upon learning of any plans for sabotage.
"Do not take the law into your own hands. If you do, how would we be any different from 'them'?" he said.

item.title: 80 pirates arrested, 115 firearms seized in Sundarbans in over 22 months
item.description:
Bangladesh Coast Guard has arrested 80 pirates and seized 115 firearms and 518 rounds of ammunition in the Sundarbans over the past 22 and a half months.
Between January 1 and November 19, the Coast Guard West Zone also rescued 135 people, including 132 fishermen held hostage by pirates, two tourists, and a resort owner.
During the same period, 64 members of several pirate gangs surrendered to the force with 48 locally made and foreign firearms, 617 rounds of live ammunition, 25 rounds of pistol ammunition and 413 rounds of airgun pellets, among other weapons and equipment.
Coast Guard media officer Lt Commander Suman Al Mukit confirmed the information, saying 63 of the operations resulted in significant arms and ammunition seizures, arrests of bandits and the rescue of abducted people.
He said intelligence surveillance and regular patrols were continuing across the vast and remote areas of the Sundarbans to prevent criminal activities and eliminate forest piracy.
Two special operations, titled “Operation Restore Peace in Sundarbans” and “Operation Mangrove Shield”, are underway to dismantle active pirate gangs and ensure the safety of fishermen, boatmen, honey collectors and other forest-dependent communities.
During the operations, the Coast Guard seized 115 locally made and foreign firearms, 10 rounds of live pistol ammunition, 518 rounds of live cartridges, 442 blank cartridges, 52 rounds of .22-calibre ammunition, 366 airgun pellets and five walkie-talkie sets from the bandits.
Members of the Chhoto Sumon, Boro Jahangir, Chhoto Jahangir and Nana Bhai gangs were among those who surrendered.
The Coast Guard said sustained operations and coordinated efforts with other law enforcement agencies had significantly weakened and fragmented the organisational strength of pirate gangs operating in the Sundarbans.
In efforts to protect wildlife and prevent deer poaching, the force also seized around 1,152kg of deer meat, 18 deer heads, four hides, 72 deer legs and a large number of hunting traps during the period. Thirty-seven people were arrested in connection with deer poaching. The seized items were handed over to the Forest Department offices for legal action.

item.title: President warns against self-destruction thru violence, calls for end to arson, terrorism
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Friday warned that the people of the country were destroying themselves through killings, arson attacks, terrorism and forced factory closures, calling for an end to such activities to move Bangladesh forward.
“Incidents of arson and terrorism, killing innocent people, setting buses on fire and forcing the closure of factories are still taking place. We must get out of this situation. No nation can achieve development by destroying itself,” he said.
The President also said the country's fundamental problems remained unresolved even decades after independence, stressing that Bangladesh could not move forward unless these problems were addressed.
He made the remarks while addressing a program as the chief guest marking the 186th founding anniversary and reunion of Dhaka College, one of the country's oldest educational institutions.
Mirza Fakhrul said Dhaka College should be developed into an institution that matches its historic legacy and status. “Whichever government is in power, it should give due importance to Dhaka College. The college must regain its position among the country’s leading institutions in terms of quality education,” he said.
The President described the college as one of the important educational institutions not only in Bangladesh but also across the subcontinent.
Students of the college have played leading roles in administration, politics, education, culture and other fields during British colonial rule, the Pakistan period and independent Bangladesh, he said. “The students of this institution have always demonstrated their merit and competence,” he added.
Expressing concern over the current academic environment and infrastructural limitations of the college, Mirza Fakhrul said there were inadequate accommodation and hostel facilities for students. “There are also insufficient facilities for a good library, laboratories and computer use. The problems of this important educational institution must be resolved quickly,” he said.
Calling for a major overhaul of the country’s education system, the President said many students graduate every year, but adequate employment and job opportunities are not being created for them.
“The education system has to be designed in a way that enables students to use their knowledge and skills effectively for the welfare of the people and the economy,” he said.
Emphasising the need to adapt education to technological changes, Mirza Fakhrul said the world had undergone a major technological revolution.
Alongside the Fourth Industrial Revolution, artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way people work and acquire knowledge, he said, adding that the younger generation is increasingly interested in using such technologies.
“Therefore, the use of information technology and artificial intelligence in education must be increased. At the same time, we have to think about how these technologies can be used for human welfare,” the President said.
He said Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman had taken initiatives to make education more development- and employment-oriented and had formed an education commission for this purpose.
Mirza Fakhrul urged the education minister to find out whether the report of that commission was still available.
During Ziaur Rahman’s tenure, initiatives had also been taken to make illiterate people literate through students, he said, adding that 50 marks had been allocated in the SSC examination for students’ participation in the programme.
On the role of teachers, the President said their responsibility went beyond classroom teaching. “Teachers have an important role in shaping students’ thinking, conscience, values and character,” he said.

item.title: Gopalganj slowly returns to normal, but fear keeps streets deserted
item.description:
Life in Gopalganj is gradually returning to normal after several days of violence, arson and crude bomb explosions linked to a lockdown called by the activities-banned Awami League. However, fear continues to keep the streets largely deserted.
No fresh incidents of violence or sabotage have been reported since the lockdown ended on Thursday night. Long-distance bus services resumed on the Dhaka-Khulna highway at 6am on Friday after remaining suspended for around 36 hours. The Dhaka-Barisal highway has also reopened, but train services remain suspended, disrupting local businesses.
Traffic Inspector Jahirul Islam Bhuiyan said buses began operating after felled trees blocking the roads were partially cleared.
Passengers and transport workers said services were running with far fewer passengers than usual because of lingering fears of vandalism and arson. Rickshaw, van and easy-bike drivers also reported poor earnings as the streets remained nearly empty.
Some pharmacies, grocery shops and food outlets reopened on Friday, but most businesses remained shut. Traders said sales were negligible and urged authorities to ensure lasting peace so they could resume normal operations.
The district witnessed several days of unrest linked to programmes by the activities-banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations. According to local administration and police sources, Tungipara Police Station came under attack on Tuesday as assailants allegedly tried to free arrested suspects. On Thursday, Muksudpur Police Station was attacked and set on fire, damaging furniture, important documents and several vehicles.
The violence also involved attacks on lawmakers’ homes, a bank and a Border Guard Bangladesh vehicle.
Amid the unrest, Gopalganj Science and Technology University suspended all classes and examinations indefinitely from next Sunday.
To maintain law and order, 27 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh and eight platoons of Ansar have been deployed. Police, Ansar and BGB personnel were seen patrolling key intersections and installations on Friday.
Deputy Commissioner said the situation was now under control following coordinated efforts by the administration and law enforcement agencies. Patrols led by executive magistrates have been strengthened at key points to protect public safety and prevent further violence.
Inspector General of Police Ali Hossain visited the district on Friday and said the overall situation appeared much better. He urged residents to help reopen the burnt police stations, stressing that the facilities served the public.
“If you burn down your own police station, how will the police work?” he asked, calling on peace-loving residents to stand against those creating unrest.
A visit to the town on Friday evening found most shops, tea stalls and usual gathering spots deserted. Residents and traders said fear persisted, with many staying indoors unless necessary. Some businesses also attributed the low turnout to the adverse weather.
Despite signs of improvement, Gopalganj remains far from its usual rhythm as residents wait for normal life to return.

item.title: IGP: Police can’t function if you burn down your own police stations
item.description:
Seeking locals’ cooperation in maintaining law and order in Gopalganj, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Ali Hossain Fakir said, “If you burn down your own police stations, how will the police maintain law and order?”
He added, “If you think police are not needed, then you will have to ensure your own security yourselves.” The IGP attended a meeting on the district's law and order situation at the circuit house in Gopalganj town on Friday. He made the remarks while responding to journalists' questions after the meeting.
Ali Hossain said: “I believe you (the people of Gopalganj) will cooperate with the police and other law enforcement agencies to maintain peace and order, and you will keep the area peaceful.”
Assessing the law and order situation in Gopalganj, the IGP said: “The overall situation looks very good as of today. It will remain good in the days ahead.”
Addressing local residents, he said: “All of you peace-loving people should take a stand against those who create unrest. The number of such people is not very large.”
Asked when the 2 burned-down police stations would resume operations, the police chief said: “Who are these police stations for? They are for you, for the public. If you burn down your own police station, how will they (the police) work? If you do not cooperate with the police, they cannot work. And if you want no police, then you will have to maintain your own law and order.”
Asked whether any operation would be conducted to arrest those involved in the recent violence, the IGP said: “The point is, the government will decide whatever the people want.”
Asked about the announcement of programmes by the Awami League, whose activities have been banned, the police chief said: “You have seen before that many continuous programmes were held, and what the consequences were. We should not have to take a strict position against you (the agitators).”
Earlier in the morning, IGP Ali Hossain Fakir, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) Director General Major General Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui, and Special Response Battalion (SRB) Director General Faruk Ahmed arrived in Gopalganj to assess the district's law and order situation following the recent violence.
The IGP then attended a special welfare meeting at Gopalganj Police Lines. From there, the police chief and the BGB and SRB directors general went to the circuit house for a meeting on the law and order situation.
Superintendents of police and assistant superintendents of police from Gopalganj and neighboring districts, including Bagerhat, Narail and Faridpur, as well as officials from the police, BGB and SRB, attended the meeting.
On their way from Dhaka to Gopalganj town in the morning, the police chief and the BGB and SRB directors general also visited the burned-down Muksudpur police station.

item.title: PM gifts sports equipment to children on his birthday
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman gifted sports equipment to a group of children and teenagers on his birthday on Friday.
He distributed the sports equipment after offering Jummah prayers at the Bangladesh Navy Central Mosque in Banani, said Prime Minister’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon.
The prime minister also enquired after the well-being of the children.
“Although it is the prime minister's birthday, he gifted sports equipment to the children and teenagers today. He also enquired about them,” Rumon said, adding that the gifts included footballs, basketballs and nets.
During the interaction, Tarique encouraged the children to play together.
The children were delighted to receive the gifts and enthusiastically wished him a happy birthday.
“Uncle, happy birthday,” they said in unison.
In response, the prime minister smiled and thanked them, advising them not to get wet in the rain as they might catch a cold.
He then bid them farewell, saying: “Assalamu Alaikum.”
The children also responded, saying: “Assalamu Alaikum, uncle.”

item.title: Three cyclones devastate Dublar Char, threaten livelihoods of 10,000 workers
item.description:
Persistent rain, rough seas and a lack of sunshine have halted fishing and left tonnes of fish rotting, threatening the livelihoods of thousands at the heart of the Sundarbans' dry-fish industry.
The sea is raging at Dublar Char, a remote island at the southern edge of the Sundarbans where the forest meets the Bay of Bengal.
Huge waves crash against the shore, strong winds sweep across the island, and relentless rain has turned once-busy fish-drying yards into scenes of distress.
The impact of three consecutive cyclones at the beginning of the dry-fish season has left nearly 10,000 fishermen, fish traders and workers at Dublar Char struggling to survive, with their livelihoods hanging in the balance.
The dry-fish season began on October 30, prompting fishermen to head to the island with fishing nets, boats and essential supplies after taking advance loans, locally known as dadan, from fish traders. But their hopes of a profitable season soon turned into hardship as one storm after another disrupted their work.
Adverse weather conditions followed Cyclone Arnab on October 31 and Cyclone Murashu on November 3. The weather deteriorated again on November 16 under the influence of Cyclone Akvan.
The first two cyclones kept fishermen from venturing into the sea until November 5. With a signal No 3 warning in force, fishing activities remained virtually suspended for the first six days of the season. Strong winds blew away tents, tore fishing nets and damaged boats, while rain ruined fish spread across drying yards.
A brief spell of favourable weather between November 5 and 15 allowed fishermen to resume fishing and dry-fish production. However, conditions worsened again on November 16 as Cyclone Akvan brought persistent rain and overcast skies, bringing fish-drying activities to a halt.
Rain and strong winds continued to lash Dublar Char on Friday morning, with large waves crashing against the shoreline. Rainwater entered many tents, soaking rice, lentils, bedding and clothes.
The rough sea has kept fishing trawlers from venturing out for the past three days. With fishing suspended, many fishermen have been left idle, their boats and trawlers anchored in the island's canals.
The biggest blow has been to fish-drying operations, which depend on prolonged exposure to bright sunshine. The sky has remained overcast for four days, while rain has continued for the past three.
What began as intermittent drizzle turned into heavy downpours over the past two days.
As a result, fish spread across drying yards are rotting in the damp conditions instead of drying, leaving a foul smell across the area. Many fishermen have been forced to discard partially dried and spoiled fish. They fear traders will refuse to buy the damaged fish or may even impose penalties if they attempt to sell them.
Kashem Ali, 55, a bahaddar (fish trader who finances fishing operations) from Alorkol, said he had never witnessed such a situation in his 20 years at Dublar Char.
"Three cyclones have hit at the very beginning of the season. Fifteen fishermen are sitting idle together. We spend Tk5,000 every day just to feed them. Where will that money come from if we cannot catch fish? How much more can we borrow from traders?" he said.
Fisherman Rafiqul Islam, 38, said he had borrowed Tk80,000 from a trader to start the season but was now unable to go out to sea.
"My debt keeps increasing while I sit idle. I cannot even send money home to my wife and children. My son calls to ask when I will send money," he said.
Habibur Rahman, 42, a fisherman from Majher Kella, said the situation had turned their expectations upside down.
"We came here to catch fish from the sea, but now the sea itself is coming to swallow us. Without sunshine, there is no way we can recover this season," he said.
For daily-wage workers, the suspension of fishing and drying operations has meant an immediate loss of income. Hiru, who works in fish cutting and drying, said he earns Tk300 a day.
"We cut and dry fish. If there is no work, there is no wage," he said.
Nearly 10,000 fishermen, bahaddars and workers are currently stationed at Dublar Char for the dry-fish season. They operate across five main fishing grounds — Alorkol, Meher Ali's Char, Majher Kella, Office Kella and Narkelbaria.
The areas produce around 30,000 to 35,000 metric tonnes of dried fish annually, meeting domestic demand and supplying export markets, including India, Myanmar and Malaysia.
However, traders said production had already fallen by nearly 70% at the beginning of this season.
"At this time last year, I had 20 maunds of fish drying at my yard. This year, I have managed to get only three maunds. Even those are rotting," a dry-fish trader said.
Khalilur Rahman, forest ranger and officer-in-charge of the Dublar Char Fishermen's Village Patrol Outpost, said the losses would affect not only the fishing community but also government revenue. Fishermen must obtain permits from the Forest Department to operate at Dublar Char.
The government collects around Tk8 crore in revenue from the island each season, he said. He warned that the three consecutive cyclones could cause a significant shortfall in revenue this year. However, he said ensuring fishermen's safety remained the top priority.
"We are repeatedly making announcements over loudspeakers, urging them not to venture into the sea," he said.
With their livelihoods under threat, affected fishermen have called for immediate government assistance, including dry-food supplies and cash support. They have also demanded an extension of repayment deadlines for dadan loans, a waiver of interest, permanent cyclone shelters at Dublar Char and access to safe drinking water.

item.title: Ex-MP Dolon, actor Tamal remanded in Dhanmondi case
item.description:
A Dhaka court has placed former Satkhira-4 lawmaker SM Ataul Haque Dolon on a seven-day remand and former Ministry of Liberation War Affairs secretary Md Mizanur Rahman and actor Md Arif Mahmud Tamal on a four-day remand each in a case filed under the Anti-Terrorism Act with Dhanmondi Police Station.
Metropolitan Magistrate Sarah Farzana Haque passed the order on Friday following a remand petition by the investigation officer.
Public prosecutor Muhammad Shamsuddoha Sumon confirmed the order.
Inspector Md Selim Reza of the Detective Branch’s Dhanmondi zonal team, the investigation officer, produced the three accused before the court and sought 10 days’ remand for each.
Defence lawyers SM Daulat-e-Khuda and Taslima Jahan Poppy opposed the remand plea and sought bail. The prosecution, represented by Sumon and Prosecutor Harun-or-Rashid, argued in favour of remand.
Dolon was arrested from Baridhara DOHS, Mizanur from Dhanmondi and Tamal from Iqbal Field in Azimpur on Thursday night.
According to the case statement, around 200 to 274 activists of the activities-banned Bangladesh Chhatra League, Awami League and Jubo League gathered in front of Rapa Plaza in Dhanmondi on May 22 to hold an anti-government procession.
When they noticed police presence, many tried to flee. Police, with help from local residents, detained several people.
The following day, Sub-Inspector Tanvir Mehedi filed a case under the Anti-Terrorism Act with Dhanmondi Police Station.
In the remand petition, the investigation officer claimed that the three accused were actively involved in the incident and had maintained contact with other suspects who remain at large.
The petition also alleged that they supplied money and weapons for anti-government and anti-state activities, collecting funds and arms from various sources before distributing them to field-level criminals and alleged terrorists.
Investigators said the three needed to be questioned to identify and arrest the absconding accused, trace the sources of funding and recover weapons.

item.title: FM Khalilur Rahman visits Rohingya camps after ICJ verdict
item.description:
United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) President and Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman visited the Rohingya refugee camps in Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, a day after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered its ruling in the genocide case against Myanmar.
He arrived at Rohingya Camp 4 in Ukhiya around 8:45am on Friday, where refugees welcomed him.
He spoke with the refugees and listened to their accounts of suffering, insecurity and their desire to return to their homeland.
During the visit, Khalilur Rahman said: "I have come to the camp this morning at a special time, on a special day and at a historic moment. Yesterday (Thursday), the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered its ruling on the genocide committed against the Rohingya people by Myanmar. This is a historic event in the court's history."
The Rohingyas view the ICJ ruling as an important step towards securing justice, international recognition and their eventual return to Myanmar.
They hope the ruling will increase international pressure on Myanmar and help pave the way for safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation.
Khin Maung, president of the United Council of Rohingya (UCR), said: "The government and people of Bangladesh saved our lives by providing us with shelter. We are grateful for that. But we do not want to remain in refugee camps forever. Our ultimate goal is to return to our homes in Myanmar. For that, citizenship, security, freedom of movement and fundamental rights must be guaranteed."
He expressed hope that Khalilur Rahman, as president of the UNGA would raise the Rohingya's plight and their aspirations for repatriation more forcefully with the international community.

item.title: Five suffer burn injuries in Mirpur warehouse fire
item.description:
Five people suffered burn injuries in a fire at a jhut (garment scraps) warehouse in the capital's Mirpur area on Thursday night.
The injured were identified as Moin, 15, Moyna, 36, Fatema, 9, Fatema, 30, and Nadira, 30. However, details about the injured were not available.
The fire broke out around 9pm at the warehouse in a house on Paridas Road of Mirpur-10, leaving five people injured.
The injured were rescued and taken to the emergency department of the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery around 12:30am on Friday.
Dr Sultan Mahmud Shikder, resident surgeon at the institute's emergency department, said all five patients sustained burns on their respiratory tract.

item.title: Bomb-like object left at Panchagarh DC office defused after 16hrs
item.description:
A bomb-like object found on the premises of the Panchagarh Deputy Commissioner's Office was defused nearly 16 hours later by the Special Response Battalion's (SRB) bomb disposal unit.
The object was detonated at a secure location around 11pm on Thursday.
An eight-point demand memorandum bearing the logo of the Awami League's district committee was later recovered from the debris.
According to administration sources, a man with his face covered left the red tape-wrapped object beside the office help desk early Thursday morning. Security was subsequently tightened, and the SRB bomb disposal unit was called in.
ASP Touhid of SRB-13 said the object was a locally made improvised explosive device (IED). A trained bomb disposal team recovered and safely detonated it.
Panchagarh Additional Deputy Commissioner Sohel Sultan Zulkarnain Kabir Steve said officials initially could not confirm whether the object was a bomb.
He added that the recovered memorandum would be sent to higher authorities, declining to disclose its contents, citing security concerns.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 13th among world's most polluted cities
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 13th among the world's most polluted cities on Friday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 115 at 10:50a on Friday.
The city's air quality was classified as ‘moderate’, indicating little to no risk to the general public, although a small number of unusually sensitive people may experience minor health effects.
According to the AQI ranking, Pakistan's Lahore topped the list with a score of 465, followed by India's Delhi with 233 and Afghanistan's Kabul with 195.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around 7 million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Seventh uranium shipment arrives at Rooppur power plant
item.description:
The seventh shipment of uranium from Russia has arrived at the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant project in Ishwardi, Pabna.
The uranium entered the project site in three specialised trucks around 6:30am on Friday, under tight security supervised by the army and coordinated with other law enforcement agencies.
With the latest shipment, a total of seven uranium consignments have arrived at the project site, including one additional fuel shipment for the first unit and six for the second unit.
According to an earlier announcement by Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom, 163 uranium assemblies for the second unit are scheduled to arrive in seven cargo aircraft. Another 48 assemblies for refuelling the first unit will be delivered in two additional cargo shipments.
In total, nine shipments of nuclear fuel are expected to arrive in Bangladesh.
Built with Russian technology and cooperation, the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has two VVER-1200 reactor units, each with a generation capacity of 1,200MW. Once both units become fully operational, they will supply a combined 2,400MW of electricity to the national grid.
Meanwhile, trial power generation has already begun at the plant's first unit. On November 17, it began supplying 350MW of electricity to the national grid on a trial basis.
The unit was successfully synchronised with the national grid at 3:16pm that day in the presence of Science and Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam. The plant generated a maximum of 375MW during the process.

item.title: Gold price cut by Tk12,815 per bhori
item.description:
Gold and silver prices have fallen again in the domestic market, with the price of 22-carat gold dropping by Tk12,815 per bhori to Tk201,109.
The new rates came into effect at 10am on Friday.
The Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus) announced the revised prices following a meeting of its Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring on Friday morning.
In a statement, the association said the prices were revised in consideration of the overall market situation following a decline in the prices of pure gold and silver in the local market.
Under the new rates, 22-carat gold is priced at Tk17,245 per gram, or Tk201,109 per bhori (11.664 grams).
The price of 21-carat gold has been set at Tk16,470 per gram, or Tk192,349 per bhori, while 18-carat gold will cost Tk14,145 per gram, or Tk164,866 per bhori.
Gold under the traditional method has been priced at Tk11,560 per gram, or Tk134,859 per bhori.
On Thursday (November 19), 22-carat gold was priced at Tk213,924 per bhori, meaning the latest revision represents a reduction of Tk12,815.
Silver prices have also been reduced.
Under the new rates, 22-carat silver will cost Tk260 per gram, or Tk3,003 per bhori.
The price of 21-carat silver has been set at Tk250 per gram, or Tk2,916 per bhori, while 18-carat silver will cost Tk215 per gram, or Tk2,508 per bhori.
Silver under the traditional method has been priced at Tk165 per gram, or Tk1,925 per bhori.
Previously, 22-carat silver was priced at Tk290 per gram, 21-carat at Tk275, 18-carat at Tk235 and traditional silver at Tk180 per gram.
Bajus said the prescribed selling prices of gold and silver jewellery already include VAT, meaning jewellers cannot charge buyers VAT separately. However, making charges will apply depending on the design and type of jewellery.
For exchanges of old gold jewellery, a 12% deduction will apply to the prescribed price after excluding making charges and the cost of stones. For purchases of old gold jewellery, the deduction will be 18%.
No additional VAT deduction is allowed in either case, the association said.
The revised prices will remain effective at all jewellery establishments across the country until further notice, Bajus added.

Ex-army officer Ziaul Ahsan’s house vandalised, set on fire
item.description:
A group of 40 to 50 people vandalized and set fire to the Barisal residence of former army officer and former director general of the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC), Major General (retd) Ziaul Ahsan, on Thursday evening.
The incident took place around 6pm at Tahura Manzil, located on Nasir Uddin Road in the Baidya Para area, adjacent to College Road in Barisal city. During the attack, windowpanes of the 3-storey building were smashed, and furniture and belongings in a ground-floor room were damaged by fire.
According to local sources, a group of 40 to 50 people entered the residence in the evening and began vandalizing it. At one point, they poured petrol into a ground-floor room and set it on fire.
After the attackers left, local residents tried to extinguish the fire. Fire Service personnel later arrived at the scene and brought the fire under control.
Ziaul Ahsan’s younger brother, former panel mayor of Barisal City Corporation and former councilor of Ward 20, Ziaur Rahman Biplob, used to live at the residence. However, he has not lived there since August 5, 2024.
Ziaul Ahsan is currently in jail, while tenants are living in the house.
Local resident Ahmed Mia said a group of people attacked and vandalized the house before setting it on fire. As a result, belongings on the ground floor were burnt.
Barisal Kotwali Model police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Monirul Islam told Dhaka Tribune: “It has not been confirmed who set fire to a room on the ground floor of the building. However, local people extinguished the fire before the police arrived. At the same time, a vehicle from the Barisal Fire Service unit also went there, but after seeing that the fire had been extinguished, they returned. The incident is being investigated.”

item.title: Actor Tomal Mahbub taken into DB custody
item.description:
Actor Tomal Mahbub has been taken into custody by the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Detective Branch (DB) and is currently being held at its Mintu Road office in the capital.
DB officials picked him up near Irani Math in the capital’s Azimpur area shortly after 10:30pm on Thursday.
DMP Additional Commissioner (DB) Md Shafiqul Islam confirmed the development but declined to disclose the reason for his detention.
